fields.Back: Very deep ocean trenches with numerous earthquakes; a series of curved trenches more or less rings the Pacific (the Ring of Fire). They mark regions of great COMPRESSION where lithosphere (crust) is consumed.

fields.Front: Define subduction, and why do trenches have earthquakes?
fields.Back: Subduction: the process by which old, dense oceanic lithosphere is forced down into Earth's interior at a trench (a convergent boundary). Earthquakes occur because they are produced by movement along fractures (faults) in the crust, and there is certainly movement going on there.

fields.Front: Who was Hugo Benioff and what did he find?
fields.Back: A Californian who developed and applied seismographs to measure earthquake locations accurately. By the mid-1950s the seismometer was good enough for him to trace earthquakes originating at ocean trenches: they defined a thin zone sloping downward from the trench away from the ocean side toward the continental plate - the descending slab of ocean floor.

fields.Front: What is a Wadati-Benioff zone, and what is an earthquake focus?
fields.Back: The inclined zone of earthquake foci that dips from an ocean trench beneath the overriding plate, marking the still-rigid descending oceanic slab. A focus is the point of origin of an earthquake.

fields.Front: What happens above a subducting slab (Fig. 14, Japan Trench)?
fields.Back: Partial melting above the descending slab feeds a volcanic island arc, with a marginal sea between the arc and the continent; shallow foci lie near the trench and deeper foci further down the slab beneath the overriding lithosphere.

fields.Front: What is the Pacific Ring of Fire?
fields.Back: The series of curved trench features that more or less ring the Pacific Ocean, outlined by concentrated earthquake foci (Fig. 13) - convergent boundaries where lithosphere is consumed, with associated volcanoes.

fields.Text: {{c1::Charles Richter}} was Benioff's co-worker and the man who eventually {{c1::perfected}} the seismograph/seismometer.
Earthquakes along a subducting slab are classed as {{c1::shallow}}-focus (near the trench), {{c1::intermediate}}-focus and {{c1::deep}}-focus, reaching about {{c1::300}} km and beyond.

{{c1::Seismic tomography}} images sinking slabs because seismic waves travel {{c1::faster}} through {{c1::colder}} material; cool ocean-floor slabs (shown {{c1::blue}}) can be traced falling toward the core-mantle boundary.

Earthquakes trace plate edges because they are produced by movement along {{c1::fractures (faults)}} in the crust; they concentrate along {{c1::subduction zones}} (convergent) and {{c1::transform faults}}.
